subject: Science and Technology
content: Animals are classified into two main groups. Vertebrates have a backbone (spine) inside their body, and are divided into five groups: Mammals (warm-blooded, have hair or fur, feed young on milk - e.g., cattle, humans), Birds (warm-blooded, have feathers, wings, and lay eggs - e.g., chickens, eagles), Reptiles (cold-blooded, have dry scaly skin, lay eggs - e.g., lizards, crocodiles), Amphibians (cold-blooded, live both in water and on land, have moist skin - e.g., frogs, toads), and Fish (cold-blooded, live in water, breathe through gills, have scales and fins - e.g., tilapia, bream). Invertebrates have no backbone, and include insects (like ants and butterflies, with six legs and three body parts), spiders (eight legs), and worms.

subject: Science and Technology
content: A life cycle shows the stages an animal goes through from birth to becoming an adult capable of reproducing. Complete metamorphosis (four stages, body changes completely) is seen in butterflies: Egg -> Larva (caterpillar) -> Pupa (chrysalis) -> Adult butterfly. Frogs undergo a similar dramatic change: Egg -> Tadpole (lives in water, breathes with gills) -> Tadpole with legs -> Adult frog (breathes with lungs, lives on land and water). Some animals, like chickens and humans, go through direct/simple development without dramatic body changes: Egg or baby -> Young -> Adult, growing larger and more developed but keeping a generally similar body shape throughout.

subject: Science and Technology
topic: Types of Plants and Seed Dispersal
content: Plants can be grouped in different ways. By size and structure: Trees (tall, woody stem), Shrubs (smaller, bushy, woody), and Herbs (soft, non-woody stems, like most vegetables). By life span: Annuals (complete their life cycle in one year, like maize), and Perennials (live for many years, like most trees). Seed dispersal means seeds being spread away from the parent plant so they have space, light, and nutrients to grow without competing with the parent. Methods of seed dispersal include: Wind (light seeds with wings or fluff, like dandelion seeds), Animals (seeds in fruit that animals eat and later excrete elsewhere, or seeds with hooks that stick to fur), Water (seeds that float, like coconuts), and Explosion (some pods burst open and fling seeds away, like some bean pods).

subject: Science and Technology
topic: Photosynthesis: How Plants Make Their Food
content: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food. Plants need four things for photosynthesis: sunlight (energy source), water (absorbed by the roots from the soil), carbon dioxide (a gas absorbed from the air through tiny pores in the leaves called stomata), and chlorophyll (the green pigment in leaves that captures sunlight energy). Using these ingredients, the plant produces glucose (a type of sugar, used as food/energy for the plant to grow) and releases oxygen as a waste product, which is then breathed in by humans and animals. This is why plants are essential to life on Earth - they produce both food and the oxygen we breathe.

subject: Science and Technology
content: The human skeleton is made of bones that give the body its shape, protect internal organs, and allow movement. The skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs, and the spine (backbone) protects the spinal cord and supports the body's posture. Joints are places where two bones meet and allow movement, such as the knee, elbow, shoulder, and hip. Muscles are attached to bones by tendons, and work by contracting (shortening) and relaxing to move body parts - muscles usually work in pairs, with one contracting while the other relaxes, allowing bending and straightening movements like at the elbow or knee.

subject: Science and Technology
topic: Types of Teeth and Dental Care
content: Humans have four types of teeth, each with a different job. Incisors (at the front) are sharp and flat, used for cutting food. Canines (pointed teeth next to incisors) are used for tearing food. Premolars and Molars (at the back, flat with ridges) are used for grinding and chewing food into smaller pieces before swallowing. Children first grow a set of milk (baby) teeth, which later fall out and are replaced by permanent adult teeth. Good dental care includes brushing teeth at least twice a day, flossing, limiting sugary foods and drinks (which cause tooth decay), and visiting a dentist regularly for check-ups.

subject: Science and Technology
content: Humans go through several general life stages as they grow: Infancy (baby, birth to about age 2), Childhood (roughly ages 2-12, a period of rapid learning and physical growth), Adolescence (the teenage years, when the body gradually grows and changes on the path to becoming an adult), Adulthood, and Old Age. Growth is measured by tracking height, weight, and general development over time, usually recorded on a growth chart during regular health check-ups. Good nutrition (a balanced diet), enough sleep, regular exercise, and a safe, caring environment all support healthy growth and development at every life stage.

subject: Science and Technology
topic: Common Diseases and How to Prevent Them
content: Diseases can be grouped into two types. Communicable (infectious) diseases spread from person to person or through insects/water, such as the common cold and flu (spread through coughs/sneezes), malaria (spread by infected mosquito bites - prevented using mosquito nets, repellents, and clearing stagnant water where mosquitoes breed), and cholera and diarrhoea (often spread through contaminated water or food - prevented by drinking clean, boiled or treated water, washing hands, and proper sanitation). Non-communicable diseases do not spread between people, such as diabetes and heart disease, often linked to diet and lifestyle. Immunization (vaccination) helps protect children from serious diseases like measles and polio by training the body's immune system to fight them before they get sick.

subject: Science and Technology
topic: HIV and AIDS Awareness and Prevention
content: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is a virus that attacks the body's immune system. If not treated, it can lead to AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome). HIV is primarily spread through contact with infected body fluids, most commonly through unprotected sexual contact or from an infected mother to her baby during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding. It can also be spread by sharing sharp objects like needles or blades that have infected blood on them. HIV is NOT spread by hugging, shaking hands, sharing food/utensils, or using the same toilet. Prevention includes: abstaining from risky behavior, using protection, and never sharing sharp objects. In Zimbabwe, many people living with HIV lead healthy lives by taking ARVs (Antiretroviral drugs) regularly, which keep the virus under control.

subject: Science and Technology
content: Safety means taking care to avoid accidents and injuries at home, school, and in the community. Common hazards include fire, sharp objects, electricity, and poisonous substances. Basic first aid is the immediate help given to an injured person before professional medical help arrives. Simple first aid steps: 1. Burns: Run cool water over the burn for at least 10 minutes. 2. Cuts: Wash with clean water and apply a clean bandage. 3. Nosebleeds: Sit up and lean forward, pinching the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes. 4. Poisoning: Do not induce vomiting; seek medical help immediately. Always tell an adult if someone is hurt.

subject: Science and Technology
content: An ecosystem is a community of living things (plants, animals, and microorganisms) interacting with each other and their physical environment (soil, water, air, climate). A food chain shows how energy passes from one living thing to another through feeding relationships. It starts with Producers (green plants, which make their own food through photosynthesis), followed by Primary Consumers (herbivores, animals that eat plants, like a rabbit), Secondary Consumers (carnivores or omnivores that eat the primary consumers, like a snake that eats the rabbit), and Tertiary Consumers (top predators, like an eagle that eats the snake). Decomposers (like fungi and bacteria) break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil to support new plant growth, completing the cycle.

subject: Science and Technology
content: Conservation means protecting and wisely using natural resources so they remain available for future generations. Ways to conserve the environment include: planting trees (afforestation), practicing sustainable farming (like crop rotation and contour plowing to prevent soil erosion), recycling materials like paper, plastic, and glass, and protecting wildlife and their habitats. Pollution is the introduction of harmful substances into the environment. Types include: air pollution (smoke from factories and vehicles), water pollution (chemicals, sewage, or litter entering rivers and dams), soil pollution (chemicals and waste damaging farmland), and noise pollution (excessive, disturbing sound). Reducing pollution protects human health, wildlife, and the overall quality of the environment.

subject: Science and Technology
content: Energy sources are grouped into two types. Renewable energy sources can be naturally replenished and will not run out, including solar energy (from the sun), wind energy, hydroelectric energy (from flowing water, like at Kariba Dam), and biomass (from plant or animal material). Non-renewable energy sources exist in limited amounts and take millions of years to form, including coal (Zimbabwe relies heavily on coal from Hwange for electricity), oil, and natural gas - these are also called fossil fuels. Using more renewable energy is important because it causes less pollution and will not run out, while non-renewable sources are limited and contribute more to environmental problems when burned.

subject: Science and Technology
topic: Simple Electric Circuits and Static Electricity
content: An electric circuit is a complete path that allows electric current to flow, usually including a power source (like a battery), wires, and a component (like a bulb or buzzer). A circuit must be a complete, unbroken loop for current to flow - if there is a break (an open switch or a loose wire), the circuit is 'open' and current cannot flow, so a bulb will not light. A switch allows you to open or close a circuit on purpose, turning a device on or off. Static electricity is a build-up of electric charge on the surface of an object, often created by rubbing two materials together (like rubbing a balloon on hair), which can cause small sparks or make objects stick together, like hair standing up after rubbing a balloon on it.

subject: Science and Technology
content: The water cycle describes how water continuously moves between the Earth's surface and the sky. Evaporation: heat from the sun turns liquid water in oceans, rivers, and dams into water vapour (gas), which rises into the air. Condensation: as water vapour rises and cools, it turns back into tiny liquid water droplets, forming clouds. Precipitation: when water droplets in clouds become heavy enough, they fall back to Earth as rain (or sometimes hail or snow in colder places). Collection: the fallen water collects in rivers, lakes, dams, and underground (groundwater), ready to evaporate again and repeat the cycle. This continuous cycle is what provides fresh water for drinking, farming, and all life on Earth.

subject: Science and Technology
topic: Sources of Water and Water Purification
content: Water sources are grouped as surface water (rivers, lakes, dams) and groundwater (found underground, accessed through wells and boreholes). Not all water is safe to drink without treatment, as it may contain harmful germs, chemicals, or dirt. Simple water purification methods used in homes and communities include: Boiling (killing most harmful germs by heating water to a rolling boil for at least one minute), Filtering (passing water through cloth, sand, or a filter to remove dirt and some germs), and Chlorination/water treatment chemicals (adding safe amounts of chemicals like chlorine to kill germs, commonly done at municipal water treatment plants). Access to clean, safe water is essential for preventing waterborne diseases like cholera and diarrhoea.

subject: Science and Technology
content: Air is a mixture of gases surrounding the Earth, mostly made up of nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%), with small amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases. Although air is usually invisible, it takes up space and has weight (this is why a balloon feels heavier when filled with air, and why wind, which is moving air, can push objects). Air is essential for life: humans and animals need oxygen to breathe, and plants need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. Air pollution, caused by smoke, dust, and harmful gases from factories, vehicles, and fires, can make air unsafe to breathe and contribute to health problems like asthma and other breathing difficulties.

subject: Science and Technology
topic: Sound: How It Travels and Its Properties
content: Sound is produced by vibrations (fast back-and-forth movements) of an object, which travel through a medium (like air, water, or solid materials) as sound waves, until they reach our ears. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum (empty space with no matter), which is why there is no sound in outer space. Pitch describes how high or low a sound is - fast vibrations produce a high pitch (like a bird chirping), while slow vibrations produce a low pitch (like a drum beat). Volume (loudness) depends on the size of the vibration - bigger vibrations produce louder sounds. Sound can also bounce off surfaces, producing an echo, which is how bats use sound to navigate and find food in the dark.

subject: Science and Technology
content: Light sources can be natural (the sun, fire, lightning) or artificial/man-made (electric bulbs, torches, candles). Light travels in straight lines, which is why objects that block light create shadows - a shadow forms on the opposite side of an object from the light source, because the object blocks the light from passing through. Shadows change size and shape depending on the position of the light source: a light source close to an object creates a larger shadow, while a light source far away creates a smaller shadow. Reflection happens when light bounces off a surface - shiny, smooth surfaces like mirrors and still water reflect light very well and clearly, while rough, dull surfaces scatter light in many directions.

subject: Science and Technology
content: A magnet is an object that attracts (pulls toward itself) certain metals, especially iron, steel, nickel, and cobalt. Every magnet has two poles: a North pole and a South pole. Like poles repel (push away) each other (North-North or South-South), while opposite poles attract (pull toward) each other (North-South). Magnets are used in many everyday devices, including compasses (a small magnetized needle that always points North, used for navigation), fridge door seals, electric motors, and speakers. Materials that are attracted to magnets (like iron and steel) are called magnetic materials, while materials like plastic, wood, glass, and paper are not attracted to magnets and are called non-magnetic materials.

subject: Science and Technology
topic: Tools and Simple Technology in Daily Life
content: Technology means using tools, machines, and knowledge to solve problems and make daily tasks easier. Simple tools used in Zimbabwean homes and farms include: the hoe (for digging and weeding), the axe (for cutting wood), the hammer (for driving in nails), and the wheelbarrow (for carrying loads, using the wheel-and-axle simple machine to reduce effort). Modern technology in daily life includes mobile phones (for communication), radios and televisions (for information and entertainment), and solar panels (converting sunlight into electricity, increasingly used in rural areas without reliable grid electricity). Choosing the right tool for a task, and using and maintaining tools safely and correctly, are important practical skills.
